entries.title: 14mm Ultra-Wide
entries.text:
14mm Ultra-Wide

Intimate wide lensExaggerated near perspective

A 14mm ultra-wide in 14mm cinematography is a very short focal length that, from a close stand, takes in a huge field and exaggerates near-to-far size. The close camera position, not the millimeter stamp alone, is what balloons a foreground face or object against a receding room.

Create this 14mm Ultra-Wide

Narrative function

Stand an arm's length from a person and a 14mm still holds the ceiling, the corridor, and the street behind them. Near masses swell.

Far walls drop away. The figure is inside a space that will not stay polite, which is why the same glass can feel intimate and confrontational at once.

It is the wrong tool for a flattering head-and-shoulders. Edge stretch cartoons ears and cheeks unless the face stays near the optical axis.

If you only wanted a body plus a readable room without heroic geometry, step back and use 24mm Wide. If the walls must bow, that is Fisheye, not a rectilinear 14mm.

How it works

Stand first, then choose glass. Park the nodal point close enough that a hand, a table, or a face owns scale, then let 14mm include the rest.

Rectilinear 14mm keeps straight lines straighter than a fisheye; remaining stretch is perspective from that close viewpoint. Keep faces off the extreme frame edges unless further stretching is intended.

Architecture will fan from the lens axis. Prompt: 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion.

When to use it

Use it when the audience must sit inside a space that is too big or too close: a face in a hotel lobby that still owns the ceiling. Do not use 14mm as a default portrait lens, or as a sticker that means wide.

Compared with similar shots

24mm Wide is the next stop: person plus place without this much ballooning. Fisheye bends those straight lines on purpose.

50mm Normal from the same close stand still crops the room out; 14mm is inclusion plus exaggeration. Forced Perspective is a staging trick along the axis; 14mm is an optical field from a close stand.

24mm WidePerson plus place, neither winning.

FisheyeThe mind is warped, or the space is a dome.

35mm Moderate WideMost narrative coverage. Human but not telephoto.

In film

The Revenant often works this close in weather so bodies and trees share one aggressive space. Birdman keeps wide glass in tight interiors so rooms never let the actors go.

Fallen Angels films faces against expanded urban night. Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas uses close wide proximity as subjective unease.

Borrow the stand and the field, not a still.

Fallen Angels 1995Faces and bodies are filmed very close against strongly expanded urban space.

Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas 1998Distorted close proximity intensifies subjective unease.

Prompt it

Name the stand and the stretch. 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion.

Say how close the camera is (arm's length, over the table, in the doorway) and keep the face near center unless edge stretch is the point. Do not write distorted as a sticker, and do not ask for oval bokeh.

Use in Video Generator

Very close wide-angle portrait of a tired night cook leaning toward the camera in a tiny kitchen. His near hand appears larger, the room stretches strongly behind him, walls remain rigid. Expressive perspective, natural facial anatomy, no fisheye circle.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Fisheye (bowed walls) or a distant 24mm Wide labeled 14mm. The tell is either curvilinear bowing or a calm environmental portrait with no looming foreground.

Fix: move close, keep lines mostly straight, let the near object own scale. Wide angle does not automatically distort a face from every distance; viewpoint is the dominant variable.

Questions

What is 14mm ultra-wide in film?

It is a very short rectilinear focal length used from a close stand so the field is huge and near objects dwarf far ones. The close camera position, not the 14mm label alone, creates that exaggeration.

14mm Ultra-Wide vs 24mm Wide

14mm from close makes foregrounds loom and rooms recede hard. 24mm still holds person plus place, but the stretch is moderate and faces survive better away from center. If the beat is reportage rather than intrusion, use 24mm.

When should I use 14mm ultra-wide?

Use it when a face or object must stay close while the surrounding world remains intrusive. Skip it for ordinary portraits, and skip it if you actually want fisheye bowing.

How do I prompt 14mm ultra-wide for AI image or video?

Write: 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion. Name the close stand. Forbid barrel distortion unless you want fisheye.

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This 14mm Ultra-Wide opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

Very close wide-angle portrait of a tired night cook leaning toward the camera in a tiny kitchen. His near hand appears larger, the room stretches strongly behind him, walls remain rigid. Expressive perspective, natural facial anatomy, no fisheye circle.

entries.title: 24mm Wide
entries.text:
24mm Wide

A 24mm wide in 24mm lens cinematography is a moderately wide prime that holds a person and a usable amount of place without extreme stretch. Body and architecture share the rectangle; neither fully wins.

Volume

Create this 24mm Wide

Narrative function

This is the environmental portrait length. You can see the hands, the floor, and the doorway, and the face still belongs to a human rather than a mural.

Reportage interiors, street coverage, and walking masters live here because the room is a partner, not a special effect. It is the wrong tool when the space should attack the face, or when the face should erase the space.

A closer 14mm will balloon the near ground. An 85mm Portrait will melt the room into stacked color.

If the beat is most narrative talk with a little extra world, 35mm Moderate Wide is the quieter default.

How it works

Stand first: usually a few feet back, not on the nose. 24mm then includes a generous field with only moderate perspective stretch on a full-frame or Super 35 sensor.

Keep the camera closer to eye height unless rank is the point; a low 24mm will still heroic the figure because of the field, not because of a power slogan. Hands and foreground furniture will read large, so place them on purpose.

Prompt: 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage.

When to use it

Use it when a person plus their place must share the frame, neither winning: a soldier in a kitchen, a walker in a street. Do not use it to fake 14mm intrusion or 85mm isolation.

Compared with similar shots

14mm Ultra-Wide from close exaggerates near-to-far size until the room attacks. 35mm Moderate Wide shows less world and less stretch, the usual storyteller step inward.

50mm Normal from the same stand crops the environment. Anamorphic is a squeeze system, not a wider 24mm.

35mm Moderate WideMost narrative coverage. Human but not telephoto.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

50mm NormalYou do not want the glass to editorialize.

In film

Children of Men often covers bodies in threatened rooms at a wide-normal that still lets geography read. The Hurt Locker does similar work in streets and interiors: person plus place, neither a poster.

Use that grammar of shared space, not a matching still.

Prompt it

Lead with body in space, not with a mood. 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage.

Name what architecture must remain (door, street, kitchen). Do not ask for extreme distortion, oval bokeh, or a melted background.

Use in Image Generator

24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage cinema.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 14mm Ultra-Wide or 35mm Moderate Wide. The 14mm tell is a looming foreground and cartoon edges.

The 35mm tell is a tighter room with the environment demoted. Fix: stand a few feet back, hold full body or three-quarter plus readable architecture, keep stretch moderate.

Questions

What is 24mm wide in film?

It is a moderately wide lens that holds a person and a usable amount of their environment without extreme near-to-far exaggeration. Body and place share the frame.

24mm Wide vs 35mm Moderate Wide

24mm includes more architecture and a little more stretch. 35mm is the common narrative step tighter: still human, less room. 24mm is reportage space. 35mm is default coverage.

When should I use 24mm wide?

Use it when the beat is person plus place, neither winning. Skip it for close portraits and for ultra-wide intrusion.

How do I prompt 24mm wide for AI image or video?

Write: 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage. Name the room. Forbid fisheye bowing and telephoto falloff.

Melies can generate this 24mm Wide

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This 24mm Wide opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

entries.title: 35mm Moderate Wide
entries.text:
35mm Moderate Wide

A 35mm moderate wide in 35mm cinematography is the common narrative wide-normal: natural perspective with a little more world than a 50mm. It is default coverage for scenes that need both face and room.

Create this 35mm Moderate Wide

Narrative function

Most talking scenes want this field. You see the listener's shoulder, a lamp, a slice of wall, and a face that does not balloon.

The glass does a little editorial work (more place than a 50) without turning the room into a character the way 24mm and 14mm do. It is the wrong tool when the location must dominate, or when the person must become the only landscape.

Street masters and kitchen two-shots often belong at 24mm. Isolation close-ups belong at 85mm.

If you shoot every size on 35mm, the coverage matches, but you never change how space feels.

How it works

Stand at a conversational distance, roughly the same as a person talking across a table or a small room. On Super 35, 35mm sits near format-normal; on full frame it is a mild wide.

Either way the perspective is gentle if you do not crowd the nose. Keep verticals honest unless a tilt is the sentence.

Prompt: 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.

When to use it

Use it for most narrative coverage that should feel human but not telephoto: a two-shot at a table, a walk through a doorway. Do not use it as the only length in a film that needs space to change meaning.

Compared with similar shots

24mm Wide shows more architecture and more stretch. 50mm Normal crops toward the conversation and editorialize less.

85mm Portrait from farther back isolates the face and stacks the background. 35mm is the middle storyteller, not a look.

50mm NormalYou do not want the glass to editorialize.

24mm WidePerson plus place, neither winning.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Moonlight often covers faces in rooms at a moderate wide-normal so Miami stays present without becoming a postcard. Manchester by the Sea does the same with New England interiors: people in places, neither squeezed nor stretched.

Grammar for default coverage, not a frame to copy.

Prompt it

Name the storyteller length and the extra world. 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.

Add the room slice (kitchen, porch, car interior). Do not write bokeh wash or ultra-wide stretch.

Use in Image Generator

35mm on [Subject], the classic storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 50mm Normal (too little room) or 24mm Wide (too much stretch). The tell is either a tight conversational crop with a melted wall, or a reportage wide with looming furniture.

Fix: conversational stand, face plus a true slice of place, mild perspective.

Questions

What is 35mm moderate wide in film?

It is the common narrative wide-normal: a little more world than a 50mm, without the stretch of a 24mm. Faces stay human and rooms stay readable.

35mm Moderate Wide vs 50mm Normal

35mm includes more of the room from the same stand. 50mm is tighter and less willing to show place. 35mm is default story coverage. 50mm is the glass that refuses to editorialize.

When should I use 35mm moderate wide?

Use it for most talk and coverage that needs face and room together. Skip it when the location should dominate or when the face should be the whole country.

How do I prompt 35mm moderate wide for AI image or video?

Write: 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50. Name a slice of the room. Forbid 14mm distortion and 85mm isolation.

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This 35mm Moderate Wide opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

entries.title: 50mm Normal
entries.text:
50mm Normal

A 50mm normal in 50mm cinematography is the conventional normal prime: from a typical stand it neither stretches near space nor stacks distant planes. The glass refuses to editorialize perspective; camera position still does all of that work.

Create this 50mm Normal

Narrative function

A 50mm is the length you pick when the sentence should sound like looking, not like a lens. Faces keep proportion.

Rooms neither rush forward nor crowd in. Conversations, over-the-shoulders, and plain singles live here because the audience is not asked to notice the optic.

It is the wrong tool when space itself must argue. A 24mm will make the room a partner.

An 85mm will make the person a landscape. From the same tripod, switching to 50mm only crops; if you wanted compression you still have to walk back, then use longer glass.

How it works

Stand first at a human talking distance. On a roughly 35mm-wide sensor, 50mm is a mild tele-normal; on full frame it is the classic still-camera normal.

Either way, keep the nodal point where a person would stand, and let the field fall out. Depth of field at 50mm is moderate unless you open very wide or get close.

Prompt: 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.

When to use it

Use it when you do not want the glass to editorialize: a talk across a table, a single that should feel observed rather than styled. Do not use it to fake telephoto isolation or wide environmental stretch from a fixed stand.

Compared with similar shots

35mm Moderate Wide shows a little more world from the same stand. 85mm Portrait requires a farther stand and starts to compress the background.

Spherical is the lens construction; a 50mm is usually spherical, but spherical is not a focal length. 24mm Wide from close is a different sentence about space.

35mm Moderate WideMost narrative coverage. Human but not telephoto.

85mm PortraitA person is the landscape.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Classical coverage often parks the 50mm on singles and over-the-shoulders so the optic disappears and performance plus blocking carry the scene. Use that as grammar: conversational distance, honest proportion, no stacked city and no looming furniture.

Prompt it

Name the refusal to stretch or stack. 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.

State camera distance (across a table, a few paces). Do not add oval bokeh, barrel distortion, or heat-haze compression.

Use in Image Generator

50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-eye perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 35mm Moderate Wide labeled as normal, or 85mm Portrait because generators treat every face as a portrait length. The tell is extra room (35) or a washed, stacked background (85).

Fix: talking-distance stand, full-face proportion, background present but not crowding.

Questions

What is 50mm normal in film?

It is the conventional normal focal length: a field that neither stretches near objects nor compresses distant planes from a typical stand. Perspective still comes from where you put the camera.

50mm Normal vs 85mm Portrait

50mm at talking distance keeps the room honest and the face unstacked. 85mm from farther back enlarges the background, thins depth of field, and isolates. 50mm is conversation. 85mm is the face as landscape.

When should I use 50mm normal?

Use it when the optic should disappear: talk, witness, plain coverage. Skip it when space must stretch, stack, or isolate.

How do I prompt 50mm normal for AI image or video?

Write: 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth. Name a talking distance. Forbid ultra-wide stretch and telephoto stack.

entries.title: 85mm Portrait
entries.text:
85mm Portrait

An 85mm portrait in 85mm cinematography is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a head-and-shoulders stays large while the background enlarges and recedes in importance. The person becomes the landscape; the room becomes stacked color and shape behind them.

Create this 85mm Portrait

Narrative function

Walk back until an 85mm fills the frame with a face. Noses stop dominating.

Ears sit in proportion. The wall behind them comes forward as a soft plane rather than a readable room.

Isolation is the job: a person is the country, and everyone else is weather. It is the wrong tool for geography.

You cannot hold a kitchen two-shot honestly at 85mm in a small room because you cannot get far enough, and if you could, the space would flatten into wallpaper. If the beat is person plus place, go to 35mm Moderate Wide or 24mm Wide.

If the beat is surveillance from across a street, you wanted 135mm Telephoto.

How it works

Stand first, farther than conversation. Restore subject size with 85mm.

That distant viewpoint is what compresses facial features and enlarges background objects; the 85mm only chooses the crop. Open the aperture if you want rapid falloff, but shallow focus is a separate choice from the length.

Keep the camera at eye height unless you mean a power tilt. Prompt: 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.

When to use it

Use it when a person is the landscape: a close-up of thought, a romantic single, a face that should not share billing with the room. Do not use it for masters, group geography, or any beat that still needs architecture as a partner.

Compared with similar shots

50mm Normal from closer keeps the room honest. 135mm Telephoto stacks even harder and feels like eavesdropping.

Shallow Focus can happen on many lengths; 85mm is a stand plus a crop, not a synonym for blur. Macro is close-focusing on a tiny object, not a portrait length.

135mm TelephotoSurveillance, sports, or stacked city.

Shallow FocusNothing else is invited.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Her often isolates faces against a soft city so the person is the only country in the frame. Portrait cinema in general uses short telephotos this way: farther stand, larger face, background as a plane.

Borrow the distance and the isolation, not a still of Joaquin Phoenix.

Prompt it

Name the farther stand and the isolation. 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.

Say head-and-shoulders, background as a soft plane, not a readable room. Do not write 24mm, and do not ask for environmental architecture in focus.

Use in Image Generator

85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, beautiful falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 50mm Normal or a wide close-up that balloons the nose. The tell is a large room still readable behind a close face, or a stretched forehead from standing too close with short glass.

Fix: walk back, 85mm, face large, background stacked and secondary.

Questions

What is 85mm portrait in film?

It is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a face stays large while the background enlarges and loses importance. The person reads as the landscape.

85mm Portrait vs 50mm Normal

50mm at talking distance still shows a honest room. 85mm from farther back compresses that room into a plane and isolates the face. Same crop size, different stand, different space.

When should I use 85mm portrait?

Use it when the face is the scene and the room should not compete. Skip it for geography, two-shots in small rooms, and environmental portraits.

How do I prompt 85mm portrait for AI image or video?

Write: 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country. Specify head-and-shoulders. Forbid wide stretch and readable architecture.

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This 85mm Portrait opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

entries.title: 135mm Telephoto
entries.text:
135mm Telephoto

A 135mm telephoto in 135mm cinematography is a long lens used from a distant stand so planes stack and the background crowds the figure. The image feels like eavesdropping: you are far away, yet the world presses in.

Volume

Create this 135mm Telephoto

Narrative function

From across a street, a parking lot, or a sports field, 135mm restores a person to usable size and collapses the air between them and whatever sits behind. Cars, crowds, and buildings become a wall.

Approaches take forever. Isolation here is not portrait softness; it is surveillance distance.

It is the wrong tool inside a small room. You cannot get far enough, and if you force it the blocking dies.

It is also the wrong tool for a tender head-and-shoulders that should still feel like a conversation: that is 85mm Portrait. If the stack must be extreme, with heat shimmer and sniper intimacy, you wanted 200mm Long Telephoto.

How it works

Walk far away first. 135mm then crops that distant view tightly.

Compression is the distant viewpoint; the long lens only chooses how much of it to keep. Expect a thin depth of field even at moderate apertures, and expect atmospheric haze or heat if the throw is long enough.

A stick or beanbag beats handheld at this length. Prompt: 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.

When to use it

Use it for surveillance, sports, or a stacked city: a figure watched from a rooftop, a runner against a wall of spectators. Do not use it for table coverage or any scene whose geography needs deep, receding space.

Compared with similar shots

85mm Portrait is the nearer telephoto: isolation without the eavesdrop. 200mm Long Telephoto is farther and harder, with more shimmer and less escape in depth.

Telephoto Compression is the perspective effect itself, which 135mm often frames. Macro is close-up scale, the opposite throw.

200mm Long TelephotoFar away and still in their pores.

85mm PortraitA person is the landscape.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

The Conversation uses long glass as listening: Harry is in the crowd and apart from it. Heat stacks Los Angeles so bodies and city occupy the same plane.

Those films treat distance as a moral fact. Borrow the throw and the stack, not a matching still.

Prompt it

Name the distant stand and the crowded background. 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.

Add across-the-street or parking-lot throw. Do not write 85mm portrait, and do not ask for wide environmental stretch.

Use in Image Generator

135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 85mm Portrait (too near, too kind) or a wide shot labeled telephoto. The tell is a readable receding street, or a close conversational background.

Fix: put the camera far away, stack the background against the body, keep the throw obvious.

Questions

What is 135mm telephoto in film?

It is a long lens used from a distant stand so depth planes stack and the background crowds the subject. The feeling is surveillance or sports distance, not a close conversation.

135mm Telephoto vs 85mm Portrait

85mm isolates a face from a portrait working distance. 135mm requires more throw, stacks the world harder, and reads as eavesdropping. 85mm is intimacy. 135mm is watching from away.

When should I use 135mm telephoto?

Use it for surveillance, sports, or a city that should press against a person. Skip it for small-room coverage and ordinary talk.

How do I prompt 135mm telephoto for AI image or video?

Write: 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure. Name the long throw. Forbid wide stretch and close-stand portraits.

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This 135mm Telephoto opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

entries.title: 200mm Long Telephoto
entries.text:
200mm Long Telephoto

A 200mm long telephoto in 200mm cinematography is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand so size differences between planes almost vanish. Heat shimmer, stacked terrain, and sniper intimacy are the physical leftovers of that throw.

Create this 200mm Long Telephoto

Narrative function

At 200mm you are often so far that the air itself becomes part of the optic: heat, dust, and haze sit in layers. A walker seems not to approach.

A face can be in their pores while the desert, the compound, or the crowd is a flat wall glued to their shoulders. It is the wrong tool for any scene that must explain left and right in a room.

It is also the wrong tool if you only wanted portrait isolation; 85mm already does that without the shimmer and the unreachable camera. If the stack is a city street rather than a desert or a sniper line, 135mm Telephoto is usually enough.

How it works

Stand very far first, then restore size with 200mm. Support the camera; angular shake is huge at this length.

Focus is unforgiving. Expect a thin slice of sharpness and, outdoors, visible atmospheric disturbance along the path.

Do not confuse this with digital zoom from a 50mm stand: that crop has no compression because you never moved. Prompt: 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.

When to use it

Use it when you must be far away and still in their pores: a desert rider, a compound watch, a face across a canyon of air. Do not use it for dialogue coverage or for a portrait you could have made at 85mm.

Compared with similar shots

135mm Telephoto is the nearer long lens, stacked but less extreme. Telephoto Compression names the viewpoint effect 200mm often shows.

85mm Portrait is intimacy from a portrait stand, not this throw. Macro is the opposite: inches, not hundreds of meters.

135mm TelephotoSurveillance, sports, or stacked city.

Telephoto CompressionThe city or army is right on their back.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Lawrence of Arabia uses heat telephotos so distant riders take an age to arrive through shimmer. Zero Dark Thirty uses long glass as watcher's distance on compounds and streets.

Grammar of throw and air, not a poster of a silhouette.

Prompt it

Name the extreme throw and the air. 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.

Say the camera is hundreds of feet away. Do not write portrait 85mm, and do not ask for a wide establishing field.

Use in Image Generator

200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 135mm Telephoto or a cropped 50mm labeled 200mm. The tell is too much remaining depth, or no atmospheric stack.

Fix: put real distance between camera and subject, let planes glue together, allow haze or heat if outdoors.

Questions

What is 200mm long telephoto in film?

It is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand. Planes stack until there is almost no escape in depth, and air or heat often sits in the image.

200mm Long Telephoto vs 135mm Telephoto

Both stack space from far away. 200mm needs more throw, compresses harder, and more often shows heat shimmer or sniper distance. 135mm is stacked city or sports. 200mm is the farther wall.

When should I use 200mm long telephoto?

Use it for desert approaches, compound surveillance, or any beat that must stay far and still read pores. Skip it for rooms, talk, and ordinary portraits.

How do I prompt 200mm long telephoto for AI image or video?

Write: 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy. State the huge throw. Forbid wide fields and close-stand faces.

entries.title: Anamorphic
entries.text:
Anamorphic

Oval bokehAnamorphic lens signature

Anamorphic cinematography squeezes one image dimension during capture, usually horizontally by 2x, then expands it for presentation. Depending on the lens, that cylindrical squeeze can produce oval bokeh, directional flares, and distinctive edge behavior; a wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic photography.

Volume

Create this Anamorphic

Narrative function

The frame can hold a face and a landscape in the same breath because the desqueezed field is wide while the taking lens may still be a moderate focal length. Highlights streak sideways.

Out-of-focus lamps become ovals. The optic announces a movie without needing black bars glued onto a spherical image.

39:1. Cropping a Spherical 50mm and adding letterbox is an aspect ratio, not this glass.

It is also the wrong tool if you need clinical edges and round bokeh. Not every anamorphic lens flares the same way; do not treat Anamorphic Flare as automatic.

How it works

8x) or recreate specific optical traits with restraint. Keep desqueezed geometry correct: circles in the world must not stay squeezed in the final image.

Focus breathing and a thinner vertical taking field are common. Oval bokeh comes from the cylindrical elements, not from a filter sticker.

Prompt: Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character.

When to use it

Use it when the frame should announce itself as widescreen glass: a night interior with oval lamps, a face in a wide city. Do not use it as a synonym for letterbox, and do not sprinkle blue streaks on every spherical shot.

Compared with similar shots

Spherical has round bokeh and rectilinear edges with no squeeze. Anamorphic Flare is one artifact some anamorphic lenses produce, not the whole system.

Vintage Cine Glass can be spherical or anamorphic; vintage is coatings and contrast, not the squeeze. Black bars on a 16:9 file are not this technique.

Anamorphic FlareNight lights and headlights should write on the lens.

SphericalControl and sharpness over romance.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Blade Runner uses anamorphic night interiors and city imagery as a widescreen optical fact. Inception's live-action photography is largely anamorphic widescreen.

La La Land and The Batman lean on oval highlights and directional flares as part of that glass. Borrow the squeeze behavior, not a copyrighted still.

Blade Runner 1982Widescreen night interiors and city imagery.

Inception 2010Much of the live-action photography uses an anamorphic widescreen approach.

Prompt it

Name the squeeze and the artifacts you actually want. Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character.

39:1 if the delivery is widescreen. Do not write letterbox on a spherical lens, and do not add random blue streaks without oval bokeh and correct geometry.

Use in Video Generator

Night exterior of a woman beneath station lights, widescreen anamorphic-style optics, subtle oval defocused highlights and restrained horizontal flare from one practical light. Natural face width, coherent architecture, no excessive streaks and no letterbox bars baked into the image.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Spherical footage with black bars, or a flare overlay without oval highlights. The tell is round lamps, no squeeze character, and a 16:9 image with mats.

Fix: oval bokeh, horizontal highlight streaks, desqueezed widescreen geometry. A wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic.

Questions

What is anamorphic in film?

It is a lens system that squeezes one dimension at capture and expands it for viewing. Many such lenses add oval bokeh and directional flares. Widescreen shape by itself is not anamorphic.

Anamorphic vs Spherical

Spherical lenses do not squeeze; bokeh is typically round and edges stay rectilinear. Anamorphic lenses squeeze, then desqueeze, and often ovalize highlights. Letterboxing a spherical image does not convert it.

When should I use anamorphic?

Use it when you want the specific optical behavior of squeeze glass: oval lamps, horizontal flares, a wide field from a moderate taking length. Skip it if you only wanted black bars.

How do I prompt anamorphic for AI image or video?

Write: Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character. Demand desqueezed geometry. Forbid round bokeh and simple letterbox.

entries.title: Spherical
entries.text:
Spherical

A spherical lens in spherical lens cinematography uses rotationally symmetric elements with no anamorphic squeeze, so the image is captured already in its display proportions. Bokeh from a round iris is round, and edges stay rectilinear aside from ordinary wide-angle stretch.

Create this Spherical

Narrative function

This is default modern capture. You pick a focal length, you stand somewhere, and the optic does not ovalize lamps or streak headlights into bars.

Sharpness and control are easier to specify because you are not also managing squeeze, desqueeze, and cylindrical artifacts. It is the wrong tool only when those artifacts are the point.

If the beat needs oval highlights and horizontal flares, you wanted Anamorphic. 39:1 still exists: you crop or use a large sensor.

That is an aspect ratio on spherical glass, not a conversion.

How it works

Choose a spherical prime or zoom and a stand. Perspective still comes from camera position; 24mm spherical is not 85mm spherical.

Keep the iris in mind if bokeh shape matters: a round iris yields round highlights; a many-bladed iris yields a polygon. No desqueeze in post.

Prompt: Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.

When to use it

Use it when you want control and sharpness over squeeze romance: most coverage, VFX plates, anything that must stitch or track cleanly. Do not label spherical footage anamorphic because you added black bars.

Compared with similar shots

Anamorphic squeezes and often ovalizes. 50mm Normal is a focal length you will often shoot spherical.

Vintage Cine Glass may be spherical glass with older coatings; vintage is not a squeeze. Fisheye is curvilinear spherical or a dedicated projection, still not anamorphic.

AnamorphicYou want the frame to announce it is a movie.

50mm NormalYou do not want the glass to editorialize.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Most modern digital cinema is spherical unless the production states otherwise. Use that as a reminder: round lamps, no horizontal streak from the taking lens, geometry that matches a prime's field.

The look is the stand and the length, not a flare pack.

Prompt it

Name the lack of squeeze. Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.

Then name the actual focal length (35mm, 50mm, 85mm). Do not add oval highlights or blue horizontal flares.

Use in Image Generator

Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Anamorphic stickers on a round-bokeh image. The tell is letterbox plus circular lamps plus random streaks.

Fix: round bokeh, no squeeze, rectilinear edges, and a named spherical focal length.

Questions

What is spherical in film?

Spherical lenses capture an unsqueezed image with rotationally symmetric optics. Highlights through a round iris stay round, and there is no anamorphic desqueeze.

Spherical vs Anamorphic

Spherical: no squeeze, typically round bokeh, rectilinear field. Anamorphic: squeeze at capture, oval bokeh, often directional flares. Cropping spherical footage to widescreen does not make it anamorphic.

When should I use spherical?

Use it as default glass when you need control, sharpness, or clean plates. Skip it only when the squeeze artifacts themselves are the sentence.

How do I prompt spherical for AI image or video?

Write: Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak. Add a real focal length. Forbid oval bokeh and horizontal flares.

Melies can generate this Spherical

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This Spherical opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.

entries.title: Fisheye
entries.text:
Fisheye

Curvilinear ultra-wide view

A fisheye in fisheye cinematography is a very wide curvilinear projection that bends straight lines, especially away from the center. The world wraps around the lens; architecture becomes a bowl rather than a rectilinear box.

Volume

Create this Fisheye

Narrative function

Put a face in the middle and the room circles them. Put them off-center and their skull stretches along the barrel.

The mapping can be circular (a round image in a black frame) or diagonal (the circle fills the rectangle). Either way, the mind of the shot is warped, or the space is a dome.

It is the wrong tool when you wanted extreme width with straight walls. That is a rectilinear 14mm Ultra-Wide.

Random wobbly architecture is a model failure, not fisheye projection. If the beat is only a mildly wide room, 24mm Wide already does it without the wrap.

How it works

Choose circular or full-frame fisheye and stage faces near the center unless edge stretching is deliberate. Keep the distortion systematic: lines bow around a stable center, they do not ripple.

A zenith or dome shot will map the room as a globe. Prompt: Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality.

When to use it

Use it when the mind is warped, or the space is a dome: a palace that should feel wrong, a subjective spiral, a helmet-cam joke. Do not use it as a synonym for 14mm, and do not apply random warping.

Compared with similar shots

14mm Ultra-Wide is rectilinear: huge field, straight-ish lines, stretch from a close stand. Fisheye is curvilinear by design.

24mm Wide is moderate and polite. Kaleidoscope multiplies fragments; fisheye is one continuous wrap.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

24mm WidePerson plus place, neither winning.

35mm Moderate WideMost narrative coverage. Human but not telephoto.

In film

The Favourite bends palace interiors under conspicuously wide, curvilinear views. Poor Things uses highly distorted wide-angle views so the world stays unfamiliar.

A Clockwork Orange and Being John Malkovich have used extreme wide wrap as subjective pressure. Grammar of bowing space, not a filter preset.

The Favourite 2018Palace interiors bend under conspicuously wide, curvilinear views.

Poor Things 2023Highly distorted wide-angle views contribute to an unfamiliar world.

Prompt it

Name the projection. Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality.

Say whether the image is a circle or fills the frame, and keep the face near center unless stretch is the point. Do not write 14mm rectilinear, and do not ask for random wobble.

Use in Video Generator

A palace official stands small at the center of an enormous ornate chamber, filmed with a frame-filling fisheye look. Walls bow smoothly toward the edges, ceiling and floor remain structurally coherent. Slow restrained action, locked camera, no circular black border.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is 14mm Ultra-Wide with extra warp, or a wavy hallucination. The tell is straight walls that should bow, or unstable rippling.

Fix: systematic barrel around a clear center, horizon curved, face protected unless you mean the stretch.

Questions

What is fisheye in film?

It is a curvilinear ultra-wide projection that bends straight lines away from the center. The field wraps around the lens instead of drawing a rectilinear box.

Fisheye vs 14mm Ultra-Wide

A 14mm rectilinear ultra-wide keeps lines mostly straight and exaggerates size from a close stand. A fisheye bows those lines on purpose. Width is not the same as wrap.

When should I use fisheye?

Use it when unreality, comedy, or a dome of space is the point. Skip it for ordinary wides and for rectilinear 14mm intrusion.

How do I prompt fisheye for AI image or video?

Write: Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality. Specify circular versus full-frame fill. Forbid random wobble and rectilinear 14mm.

entries.title: Tilt-Shift
entries.text:
Tilt-Shift

Tilt-shift lookDiorama illusion

Tilt-shift cinematography tilts the lens relative to the sensor so the plane of focus rotates, and may also shift the lens to slide perspective. A narrow band or shaped region of sharpness, often from a high viewpoint, can make a real-scale scene resemble a small model.

Volume

Create this Tilt-Shift

Narrative function

Tilt is not a blur sticker. The Scheimpflug relation puts a slice of the world in focus along a plane that is no longer parallel to the sensor: a street of rowers, a crowd, a tabletop of people who suddenly read as toys.

Shift is a different job: it slides the image to keep verticals parallel or to look around a corner without rotating the camera. It is the wrong tool when you only wanted a face isolated from a wall.

That is Shallow Focus on a normal plane. It is also the wrong tool if the miniature effect has no high viewpoint and no consistent focus band.

A horizontal blur strip that ignores perspective is a post fake, not this optic.

How it works

Tilt the lens so the focus plane cuts through the subject as a thin band or a wedge. A high angle helps the diorama reading because we look down on models.

Match blur to depth; as perspective changes, the band should follow the plane, not a 2D stripe. Shift independently if you need to correct converging buildings.

Prompt: A real-scale city or citadel with [Subject] human-sized. A thin band of focus across the subject, foreground and far ground softly blurred, no hard seam across the frame.

When to use it

Use it to make a city a model, or to slice focus through a crowd on a tilted plane. Do not use it as a synonym for shallow portrait focus, and do not lay a blur bar across a flat image.

Compared with similar shots

Shallow Focus keeps the focus plane parallel to the sensor and isolates by distance. Tilt rotates that plane.

Macro is close-up scale, not a diorama of a city. Bird's-Eye View can supply the high viewpoint the miniature reading often needs, but a bird's-eye without a tilted focus plane is just a map.

Shallow FocusNothing else is invited.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

24mm WidePerson plus place, neither winning.

In film

The Social Network's Henley rowing sequence gives real-scale action a miniature-like appearance through a thin, high, diorama focus. Miniature-city treatments in other films follow the same grammar: high view, shallow band, motion that reads like a toy.

Borrow the plane, not a still of the race.

The Social Network 2010The Henley rowing sequence gives real-scale action a miniature-like appearance.

Prompt it

Name real scale, then the thin focus plane. A real-scale city or citadel with [Subject] human-sized.

A thin horizontal band of focus across the subject, foreground and far ground softly blurred, no hard seam across the frame. Add a high viewpoint if you want the diorama.

Do not write shallow bokeh portrait, and do not ask for a hard blur stripe.

Use in Video Generator

High oblique view of two rowing teams moving along a river, with a narrow depth-aware focus region around the boats and smoothly increasing blur nearer and farther away. Slightly brisk motion and crisp miniature-like detail. No actual toy proportions, no arbitrary blurry stripe across faces.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Shallow Focus on a face, or a post miniature with a 2D blur strip. The tell is a portrait with creamy background, or a seam that ignores buildings' depth.

Fix: high view, human-sized figures, focus as a plane through the scene, blur that follows depth.

Questions

What is tilt-shift in film?

Tilt rotates the plane of focus relative to the sensor. Shift slides the lens to change perspective without tilting the camera. Together they can isolate a band of sharpness or make real scenes read as models.

Tilt-Shift vs Shallow Focus

Shallow focus keeps the focus plane parallel to the sensor and falls off with distance. Tilt-shift can put a wedge or band of focus through a scene, including a high diorama view of a city. Blur shape is the difference.

When should I use tilt-shift?

Use it to slice focus through a crowd or to turn real-scale action into a model. Skip it for ordinary portraits that only need a fast 85mm.

How do I prompt tilt-shift for AI image or video?

Write that the subject is human-sized in a real city, with a thin band of focus and no hard seam. Add a high viewpoint for the diorama. Forbid a flat blur stripe and ordinary portrait bokeh.

entries.title: Macro
entries.text:
Macro

Extreme-detail photographyPlan macro

Macro cinematography is close-focusing optics that let a small object or surface occupy the image at high reproduction scale, often near 1:1. An unusually close view turns texture, insects, eyes, or mechanisms into the entire shot.

Volume

Create this Macro

Narrative function

The plot becomes a centimeter. A pill, a watch gear, a drop, a pupil: the object is no longer an insert in a room, it is the room.

Depth of field collapses to a millimeter, so a breath or a rack is a traverse across a landscape of pores. It is the wrong tool when you only wanted a tight face.

An Extreme Close-Up of an eye can be a long lens from a foot away; that is a crop, not macro scale. A normal close-up enlarged in post does not automatically have convincing macro texture or depth of field.

If you need to travel through a glass or a machine, that is a Probe Lens.

How it works

Use a macro lens or close-focus setup, stabilize the object, and light for surface texture (small hard sources show relief; wrap shows translucency). Anticipate shallow depth of field and tiny focus changes.

Working distance is short; watch your own shadow. Magnification is image size over object size, not the shot-size name.

Prompt: Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], insects of texture, an eye, a watch, a drop of rain, a world in a centimeter.

When to use it

Use it when the plot is microscopic: a ritual of pills, a bug, a lock mechanism. Do not use it as a synonym for close-up, and do not blow up a normal portrait and call it macro.

Compared with similar shots

Extreme Close-Up is a framing size; it may or may not use macro optics. Insert Shot is a story object in the cut, any size.

Probe Lens is a long barrel that can enter tiny spaces with a wide-ish view. Magnification is the scale number; macro is one optical way to get it.

Extreme Close-UpA detail is the scene: an eye, a mouth, a trigger.

Insert ShotPoint at the thing that will matter later.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Requiem for a Dream repeats extreme-detail images so rituals compress into sensory fragments. Amélie turns ordinary objects into tactile small pleasures.

Microcosmos treats insects as full-scale drama. Grammar of close-focus scale, not a copied frame of a pupil.

Requiem for a Dream 2000Repeated extreme-detail images compress rituals into sensory fragments.

Amélie 2001Tactile details turn ordinary objects and actions into small pleasures.

Prompt it

Name the optic and the centimeter. Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], insects of texture, an eye, a watch, a drop of rain, a world in a centimeter.

State 1:1 or similar scale, razor-thin focus, real surface texture. Do not write close-up of a face unless the face feature is truly macro-scaled.

Use in Video Generator

Extreme macro shot of a watchmaker lowering one tiny screw into an old brass mechanism. The screw head and adjacent gear teeth are crisp; focus falls away rapidly. One slow precise movement, realistic metal scale, no oversized fingers or morphing gears.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Close-Up made with a portrait lens, or a zoomed crop. The tell is normal skin-pore size with deep-ish focus, or a whole face labeled macro.

Fix: small object filling the sensor, true close-focus falloff, texture lit as terrain.

Questions

What is macro in film?

It is close-focusing photography that reproduces a small object at high scale, often around life-size on the sensor. Texture and tiny depth of field become the image.

Macro vs Extreme Close-Up

An extreme close-up is a crop of a feature, possible with a long lens from a foot away. Macro is an optical scale: a small object occupies the frame at high magnification with true close-focus depth of field.

When should I use macro?

Use it when a tiny object or surface is the scene. Skip it for ordinary portraits and for inserts that are merely tight, not close-focus.

How do I prompt macro for AI image or video?

Write: Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], a world in a centimeter, razor-thin focus, surface texture. Name the object. Forbid ordinary close-up and probe-through-a-tunnel unless you want those.

Melies can generate this Macro

Melies is the AI filmmaking workspace. This Macro opens with the optical prompt loaded, so you get glass behavior instead of a lens name as decoration.

Extreme macro shot of a watchmaker lowering one tiny screw into an old brass mechanism. The screw head and adjacent gear teeth are crisp; focus falls away rapidly. One slow precise movement, realistic metal scale, no oversized fingers or morphing gears.

entries.title: Probe Lens
entries.text:
Probe Lens

A probe lens is a long, narrow macro optic that can pass through small spaces and create extreme close moving shots from inside the subject. The front element is tiny and far from the camera body, so the viewpoint can enter a glass, a wound of machinery, food, or a miniature set.

Create this Probe Lens

Narrative function

The camera body stays outside. The tube goes where a camera cannot: through ice in a drink, between gears, across a tabletop forest, into a bottle.

The view is often wide at the tip, so a drop of liquid becomes a lake and a crumb becomes a boulder, while the move can travel through that world. It is the wrong tool when a standard Macro from outside already sees the surface you need.

It is also the wrong tool for a face portrait; the look is proximity through a hole, not an 85mm single. If you only wanted a 14mm in a normal room, you wanted 14mm Ultra-Wide, not a probe.

How it works

Mount the probe, protect the barrel, and plan a path the tip can physically travel. Light from outside the tiny space or fiber the interior; the front element is close to the subject and will see your flags if you are careless.

Depth of field is still small despite the typical slow stop, because you are close. Stabilize the move; inches are miles.

Prompt: Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.

When to use it

Use it to go where a camera body cannot: through a drink, into a watch, across a plated meal as if it were terrain. Do not use it as a synonym for macro on a tabletop you could shoot from above.

Compared with similar shots

Macro photographs a small object from outside at high scale. A probe enters the space.

14mm Ultra-Wide is a wide field from a normal camera body. Magnification is the scale; the probe is a delivery system that also tends to be wide at the tip.

MacroThe plot is microscopic.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

24mm WidePerson plus place, neither winning.

In film

Commercial food and product work uses probes constantly so a camera can travel through bubbles and garnish. The Hobbit's miniature-language cousins (and similar tabletop/miniature photography) rely on tiny viewpoints inside constructed worlds.

Treat those as grammar for impossible proximity, not as a still to copy.

Prompt it

Name the tube and the interior path. Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.

Describe the path (through the ice, between gears). Do not write 85mm portrait or ordinary overhead macro.

Use in Image Generator

Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Macro from outside, or a 14mm in a full-size room. The tell is a tabletop still with the camera clearly outside, or a normal interior wide.

Fix: viewpoint from inside a small space, barrel-path move, wide-at-the-tip scale.

Questions

What is a probe lens in film?

It is a long, narrow close-focus optic whose tiny front element can enter small spaces. You get extreme proximity and, often, a wide view from inside an object or miniature set.

Probe Lens vs Macro

Macro is close-focus from outside: a lens aimed at a small object. A probe is a barrel that can pass through that object or between objects, with the camera body remaining outside the tiny space.

When should I use a probe lens?

Use it when the shot must travel through a drink, a machine, food, or a miniature gap a camera body cannot enter. Skip it if a normal macro from outside already sees the surface.

How do I prompt a probe lens for AI image or video?

Write: Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world. Name the path through the space. Forbid ordinary portraits and overhead macros.

entries.title: Split Diopter
entries.text:
Split Diopter

Split-field diopterDouble plan de netteté

A split diopter is a partial close-focus element that keeps different distance zones sharp in one frame. One region focuses very near while another remains focused farther away; it is not two focal lengths, and it is not ordinary deep focus.

Volume

Create this Split Diopter

Narrative function

A telephone in the foreground and a doorway across the room can both be tack-sharp, with a narrow blur band where the half-lens ends. The construction is often hidden on a door edge, a lamp, or a dark seam.

The coexistence is the sentence: a face and a distant threat are equally true at once. It is the wrong tool when a small aperture and careful staging would hold both planes without a seam.

That is Deep Focus. It is also the wrong tool if you meant to throw attention from one plane to the other over time: that is Rack Focus.

Do not describe this as a split-screen or a ghost overlay.

How it works

Mount a split-field diopter in front of the taking lens so half the field is a close-up filter. Focus the naked side on the far subject; the diopter side will bring a near object into focus.

Hide the boundary against a vertical edge or a soft region. A two-focus composite can recreate the look with more control.

Prompt: One continuous room: a near object on the left tack-sharp and [Subject] far on the right also tack-sharp, a narrow blur band between them. Not a split-screen, not a ghost overlay.

When to use it

Use it when two distances must both be true at once: a listener and a far figure, a glass and a door. Do not use it as a substitute for deep focus, and do not split the frame into two movies.

Compared with similar shots

Deep Focus holds near and far by stopping down and staging, with no diopter seam. Rack Focus changes which plane is sharp over time.

Split Screen cuts the frame into separate images. A split diopter is one take, two focus regions, a possible tell at the join.

Deep FocusLet the audience find the story in the whole room.

Rack FocusChange who owns the shot without cutting.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Blow Out holds near listening equipment or faces with distant action in the same composition. Jaws keeps near and far figures simultaneously sharp in selected setups.

The Conversation and Mission: Impossible have used the same charged coexistence. Grammar of two distances at once, not a copied still.

Blow Out 1981Near listening equipment or faces share the frame with distant action.

Jaws 1975Near and far figures are held simultaneously in focus in selected compositions.

Prompt it

Name one room and two sharp zones. One continuous room: a near object on the left tack-sharp and [Subject] far on the right also tack-sharp, a narrow blur band between them.

Not a split-screen, not a ghost overlay. Hide the join on a door or pole.

Do not write deep focus or two shots side by side.

Use in Video Generator

A listening device fills the near-left foreground; a suspicious figure stands far back on the right. Both are tack sharp, with a narrow soft transition aligned to a dark door jamb between them. Locked camera, deliberate split-diopter look, not uniformly sharp depth throughout the room.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is Deep Focus (no seam, everything held by aperture) or Split Screen (two images). The tell is a hard vertical cut, a double-exposed ghost, or uniform focus with no join.

Fix: two distance zones, both sharp, a narrow optical blur band, one continuous space.

Questions

What is a split diopter in film?

It is a partial close-up lens that lets one part of the frame focus very near while another part stays focused far away. The join often shows as a thin blur band.

Split Diopter vs Deep Focus

Deep focus uses a small aperture and staging so a single focus field covers near and far. A split diopter creates two different focus regions with an optical join. It is not two focal lengths and not a split-screen.

When should I use a split diopter?

Use it when a near object and a far figure must both be sharp at once and ordinary depth of field cannot hold them. Skip it if deep focus or a rack would tell the truth better.

How do I prompt a split diopter for AI image or video?

Write one continuous room with a near object and a far subject both tack-sharp and a narrow blur band between them. Forbid split-screen, ghost overlay, and ordinary deep focus.

entries.title: Vintage Cine Glass
entries.text:
Vintage Cine Glass

Vintage cine glass is older motion-picture optics whose coatings, contrast, and aberrations differ from modern clinical primes. Lower contrast, gentle halation, and sometimes swirling or rolling edges are properties of the lens, not a grade slapped on sharp digital.

Create this Vintage Cine Glass

Narrative function

Put a face on Cooke, K35, or similar older glass and the image rolls off instead of biting. Highlights bloom a little.

Contrast sits down. Backgrounds can swirl or breathe at the edges.

Memory, period, or beauty over resolution is the job of the optic, before anyone touches the timeline. It is the wrong tool when you need hard edges for VFX or a documentary fact.

It is also the wrong tool if you only wanted a faded grade on modern glass: that is Filmic Faded or a Vintage treatment, not this lens. Halation can be stock or a filter; vintage cine may contribute similar bloom, but the swirl and the contrast live in the glass.

How it works

Choose actual vintage or vintage-inspired cine primes and shoot them wide enough to show the aberrations. Do not stop down until they behave like modern glass if those aberrations are the point.

Keep skin highlights just hot enough to halate. Separate this from anamorphic squeeze: many vintage cine lenses are Spherical.

Prompt: Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness.

When to use it

Use it for memory, period, or a face that should not look like a catalog. Do not use it as a synonym for a faded LUT on a modern zoom.

Compared with similar shots

Anamorphic is a squeeze system; some vintage glass is anamorphic, most of this entry is about spherical old coatings. Halation is highlight bloom, one trait.

Filmic Faded is a print-emulation grade. Vintage is a whole period treatment.

Vintage cine is the taking lens.

HalationHighlights should bleed like film, not clip like video.

AnamorphicYou want the frame to announce it is a movie.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

The Master and Phantom Thread are often cited for older or character glass on faces: lower bite, gentle bloom, a refusal of clinical digital edges. Use that as grammar for optic character, not as a still to match pixel for pixel.

Prompt it

Name the glass, not a sticker. Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness.

Add spherical unless you also want anamorphic ovals. Do not write faded LUT only, and do not add heavy grain as a substitute for the lens.

Use in Image Generator

Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 romance, not clinical sharpness.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a Filmic Faded grade or a Vintage dye fade on sharp modern glass. The tell is crunchy edges with a brown LUT, or grain with no optical swirl or halation.

Fix: lower contrast in the taking image, gentle highlight bloom, edge character from the lens.

Questions

What is vintage cine glass in film?

It is older motion-picture lenses with coatings and aberrations that lower contrast, bloom highlights, and sometimes swirl the edges. The character is optical, not only a grade.

Vintage Cine Glass vs Filmic Faded

Filmic faded is a print-emulation grade: lifted blacks, rolled highlights. Vintage cine is the lens: coatings, swirl, optical bloom. You can have one without the other.

When should I use vintage cine glass?

Use it when the taking optic should be gentler than modern primes: memory, period, a face that should not look clinical. Skip it for hard VFX plates.

How do I prompt vintage cine glass for AI image or video?

Write: Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness. Forbid LUT-only fade and anamorphic squeeze unless you want those too.

entries.title: Telephoto Compression
entries.text:
Telephoto Compression

Distant viewpointCompressed perspective

Telephoto compression in lens compression cinematography is the perspective effect of a distant viewpoint: size differences between separated depth planes shrink, so a crowd or a city appears to press against a person. A long lens then frames that distant view tightly; a long lens from a close stand does not create the effect.

Create this Telephoto Compression

Narrative function

Walk away until a far building and a near figure occupy similar size, then crop with 135mm or 200mm. Escape routes in depth disappear.

An approaching rider takes an age. A fallen body and a car can look glued together.

The air gets crowded even when the location is huge. It is the wrong tool when space should recede.

From close with wide glass, near objects balloon and far walls drop away, the opposite sentence. Do not zoom in from a fixed tripod and call it compression: that is only a crop.

Stand first, then glass.

How it works

Move farther away until the relative sizes of planes collapse, then choose a long focal length to restore the subject's size in the frame. Keep atmospheric haze, foreground overlaps, and focus consistent with that distance.

A 200mm from 50 meters compresses; a 200mm crop of a 35mm file shot from 3 meters does not. Prompt: Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth.

When to use it

Use it when the city, army, or terrain should sit right on their back: a walker who cannot outrun the buildings. Do not use it as a synonym for any long lens, and do not claim compression from a close stand.

Compared with similar shots

200mm Long Telephoto and 135mm Telephoto are lengths that often frame this viewpoint. Compression is the standpoint, not the millimeter number.

85mm Portrait starts the stack but still feels like a portrait distance. 14mm Ultra-Wide from close is the anti-compression: exaggerated size differences.

200mm Long TelephotoFar away and still in their pores.

135mm TelephotoSurveillance, sports, or stacked city.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Lawrence of Arabia lets Sherif Ali approach through desert shimmer as a study in collapsed distance. Payback glues a fallen figure and a car in depth.

Heat and Chungking Express stack cities so people have no air behind them. Grammar of viewpoint, not a copied composition.

Lawrence of Arabia 1962Sherif Ali’s distant approach through the desert shimmer.

Payback 1999A fallen figure and a car appear tightly related in depth.

Prompt it

Name the collapsed distances, not only the lens. Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth.

State a far camera. Do not write 14mm, and do not crop a close-stand wide and call it compression.

Use in Video Generator

From far away with a long lens, frame one cyclist approaching along a straight road. Successive streetlights appear densely stacked behind him and his approach seems slow despite steady pedaling. Heat shimmer, fixed camera, no wide-angle expansion or zoom.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is a long-lens label on a close-stand shot, or a wide that still shows receding space. The tell is large size differences between near and far, or a cropped 35mm perspective.

Fix: walk away, long glass, planes of similar apparent size, crowded air.

Questions

What is telephoto compression in film?

It is the flattening of size differences between depth planes caused by a distant camera position. A long lens then tightly frames that view. The lens alone, from a fixed stand, does not change perspective.

Telephoto Compression vs 200mm Long Telephoto

200mm is a focal length. Compression is what a distant stand does to planes, often framed with 135mm or 200mm. You can shoot 200mm from too close and get no stack. You can compress with other long lengths if you walk far enough.

When should I use telephoto compression?

Use it when a crowd, city, or landscape should press against a person, or when an approach should seem never to arrive. Skip it when space must recede.

How do I prompt telephoto compression for AI image or video?

Write: Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth. Demand a far camera. Forbid wide close-stand perspective.

entries.title: Magnification
entries.text:
Magnification

Magnification in magnification cinematography is the ratio of the subject's image size on the sensor to its real size. High magnification makes a centimeter of the world fill the frame; it is a scale number, not a shot-size name and not automatically a macro lens.

Create this Magnification

Narrative function

Scale is lost on purpose. A tick, a spark, a cell of fabric becomes geography.

Powers of Ten is a ladder of magnification: each step changes what counts as a place. Going closer than a close-up is the beat, but closer optically, not only by cropping a 4K face.

It is the wrong tool when you meant a Close-Up of an actor from a meter away. That face may fill the frame at low magnification.

It is also the wrong tool if the path through a tiny space is the point: Probe Lens delivers that path. Macro is the usual optic that reaches 1:1; magnification is the measurement you are after.

How it works

Decide the reproduction ratio (1:2, 1:1, 2:1) and pick optics that can hold it: macro, bellows, probe, or microscope. Light for the new scale; apparent motion and camera shake scale up with magnification.

Depth of field collapses. Do not confuse digital punch-in with optical magnification: extra pixels are not extra scale.

Prompt: Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.

When to use it

Use it when you must go closer than a close-up in true scale: a world inside a centimeter. Do not use it as a synonym for a tight portrait or a cropped still.

Compared with similar shots

Macro is close-focusing optics that commonly reach these ratios. Probe Lens adds a barrel that can enter the small world.

Extreme Close-Up is a framing of a feature, which may be low magnification. Magnification is the scale, not the cutaway name Insert Shot.

MacroThe plot is microscopic.

Probe LensGo where a camera body cannot.

14mm Ultra-WidePut the audience inside a space that is too big or too close.

In film

Microcosmos treats insect scale as full drama, true high magnification. Powers of Ten makes magnification itself the structure, stepping in and out of orders of size.

Use those as grammar for scale, not as frames to duplicate.

Prompt it

Name the lost scale. Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.

State a ratio if you can (1:1). Forbid ordinary close-up of a face, and forbid a simple crop of a wider shot.

Use in Image Generator

Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.

What usually goes wrong

The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Close-Up or a punched-in Close-Up. The tell is a whole eye from portrait distance with moderate depth of field.

Fix: object scale on the sensor near life-size or greater, razor focus, centimeter geography.

Questions

What is magnification in film?

It is the ratio of image size on the sensor to the object's real size. High magnification fills the frame with a tiny piece of the world. Shot-size names like close-up do not guarantee that ratio.

Magnification vs Macro

Macro is a class of close-focusing lens, often able to reach 1:1. Magnification is the number you get. A probe or a microscope can magnify too. A portrait close-up of a face is usually low magnification.

When should I use magnification?

Use it when true scale must collapse to a centimeter or less. Skip it when you only needed a tight crop of a person.

How do I prompt magnification for AI image or video?

Write: Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose. Name the object and, if possible, 1:1. Forbid ordinary close-ups and simple punch-ins.
